title: Jaspal Rana, India's Greatest Commonwealth Games Athlete and Manu Bhaker's Coach, Dies at 49
excerpt: The pistol shooting legend and Dronacharya Award-winning coach suffered a fatal cardiac emergency after falling ill during the ISSF World Cup in Munich
body:
Jaspal Rana, the most decorated Indian athlete in Commonwealth Games history and the coach who guided Manu Bhaker to her historic double bronze at the 2024 Paris Olympics, died on Thursday night at Max Hospital in New Delhi. He was 49.

Rana had felt chest discomfort during the ISSF World Cup in Munich, where he was serving as India's high-performance pistol coach. He initially mistook the symptoms for acidity and continued with his travel plans, his brother Subash Rana told the media. But the pain returned on the flight back to India, and he was rushed from the airport directly to the hospital, where he underwent a stent procedure. He did not recover.

"It is a huge loss. He was not only a champion shooter but also a great mentor. He will be deeply missed," said National Rifle Association of India president Kalikesh Narayan Singh Deo.

The Indian contingent had just won four medals — two gold and two silver — at the Munich World Cup under Rana's coaching, making it the final triumph of an extraordinary career spent first in competition and then in the service of the next generation.

## From Uttarakhand prodigy to world record holder

Born in 1976 in a Garhwali family in Uttarakhand, Rana was introduced to shooting by his father Narayan Singh Rana, a 1971 war veteran who went on to become the state's first sports minister. By 12, Jaspal had won a silver at the National Shooting Championship. By 18, he was a gold medallist at the 1994 Asian Games in Hiroshima and the youngest recipient of the Arjuna Award that year. By 21, he held a Padma Shri.

His trophy cabinet is staggering. Across four editions of the Commonwealth Games — Victoria 1994, Kuala Lumpur 1998, Manchester 2002, and Melbourne 2006 — Rana amassed 15 medals: nine gold, four silver, and two bronze. No Indian athlete has matched that haul. At the 2006 Asian Games in Doha, he won three gold medals and a silver, equalling the world record in the 25-metre centre-fire pistol with 590 points. In total, he won eight Asian Games medals across three editions.

He represented India at the 1996 Atlanta Olympics, competing in the 10-metre air pistol and 50-metre free pistol events — a rare Olympic appearance for Indian shooting at a time when the sport received scant attention and even less funding.

## The coach who built India's pistol pipeline

<instagram url="https://www.instagram.com/p/DZex7yxsn0N/" />

After hanging up his competitive boots, Rana channelled his precision into coaching. Beginning around 2012, he rebuilt India's junior pistol programme from the ground up, instituting training routines that replicated the pressure of Olympic matches in daily practice.

His most celebrated partnership was with Manu Bhaker. The two began working together in 2018, briefly parted ways in 2021, and reunited in 2023 with renewed purpose. At the Paris Olympics, Bhaker won two bronze medals — a first for any Indian athlete at a single Games — and publicly credited Rana as the architect of her success. "It's the sweat and blood of both of us," she said after Paris.

Beyond Bhaker, Rana mentored Saurabh Chaudhary, Anish Bhanwala, and Chinki Yadav, creating a pipeline of young Indian shooters who now compete credibly at the highest level. In 2020, he received the Dronacharya Award — India's highest coaching honour — in the same year that Bhaker and Chaudhary received their Arjuna Awards.

## A loss felt from Delhi to the diaspora

Union Defence Minister Rajnath Singh — whose family is related to the Ranas through marriage — called himself "stunned and grief-stricken." He wrote on X: "Jaspal played a highly influential role in popularising shooting as a sport in India. His passing is a great loss to the Indian sports world."

For millions of Indians abroad who grew up watching Rana's gold-medal runs through the 1990s and 2000s, the loss strikes a particular chord. He was among the first Indian athletes to dominate a non-cricket sport on the global stage, proving that India could produce world-class marksmen. His protégée Bhaker, now a household name among NRI communities who tracked her Paris journey closely, is the living continuation of that legacy.

Rana was also involved in advocacy, most notably campaigning against the 28 percent GST on imported sports equipment in 2017 — a burden that disproportionately affected athletes from middle-class backgrounds. The government eventually granted a tax exemption.

He is survived by his wife Aarushie Verma, a national-level shooter and environmentalist, and his siblings Sushma Singh and Subash Rana, both accomplished shooters in their own right. The shooting runs deep in the Rana family. Now, its greatest champion is gone.
